body:
The maintainer reported this in chat on 2026-11-20:

> Most machinists define their WCS at the center of a part or at a corner in a mill. This doesn't mean that the cutter starts from that WCS point, it just means that it references it. The fault would be that the cutter moves to the starting point as a first move. It doesn't have to. This is a general post-processing problem and operations calculation issue. The machine should move to its first starting point for an operation, in relation to the WCS, not start at the WCS. It doesn't matter where the WCS is. The first operation starts where it has to start to clear the part, but in relation to the WCS.

What the maintainer sees: the first move of an operation goes to the WCS origin (X0 Y0). It does not go to the start point that the operation needs.

Expected:
- The WCS is only the reference of the coordinates. It is not a point that the tool must visit.
- The first positioning move of each operation goes to the real start point of that operation: the entry position that clears the part and the stock.
- That point is written in coordinates of the WCS of the setup. It is correct for any WCS position (part center, corner, or elsewhere).

Why P1: a first move to a wrong point can move the tool into the part, the stock or the fixture at rapid. This is wrong output (Prime Directive).

Not known yet. The research answers these questions in comments:
- Where the defect shows: the toolpath in the viewport, the simulation, the CL file, the posted G-code, or several of these.
- If it is in the operation calculation (the first point of the toolpath), in the post (the initial move or the safe-start block), or in both.
- If it depends on the operation type, the entry type, the machine file, or the post dialect.
- If it is the same fault as the retired #2382 (coordinates measured from the world origin), or a different one. #2382 was about the origin of the coordinates. This issue is about the first move target.
- Which test or fixture proves it: a part with its WCS at the center and a part with its WCS at a corner, with the same operation.

Done means: a pinning test per operation family shows that the first move goes to the entry point of the operation in WCS coordinates, and not to X0 Y0, for a WCS at the center and at a corner. The research comment lists the files and the sub-issues.

Related: #2382 (closed).

- rapid move 119 travels through stock (below the clearance plane, or at it below the stock top)

Circular must generate safe links between its radial passes, or refuse the parameters before generation with a named cause.

A 5 mm radius with the same tool and plunge entry generates without warnings. The catalog uses this size.

body:
Request: a CamCraft user ("Chang Frick" on the SolidCraft Discord #camcraft channel) runs EMCO machines in his garage: an EMCO VMC-200 mill and an EMCO Turn 342 lathe with Siemens Sinumerik controls, plus two VMC-200s being converted to LinuxCNC. His mill control is a **Sinumerik 810M**, an older system. Our only Siemens post, `assets/posts/sinumerik.cps`, targets the **840D**, whose dialect is newer (for example cycle calls, frames and the program header differ).

He offered to help test. He suggested ISO 6983-1 as the starting point.

Clean-room note: he made his own post for Fusion 360. Do not ask for it, read it or use it, and do not read G-code that Fusion produced (AGENTS.md "Clean-Room Protocol": no post processors or output from that product line). Write the post only from public sources: ISO 6983-1, Siemens' published Sinumerik 810M/820M programming documentation (behaviour only), and machine-tool handbooks.

What to find out (in this issue, before code):
- What differs between the 810M and the 840D for 3-axis milling: program start and end, `%` and program numbers, tool change (T/D/M6), offsets (G54-G57, G158/G159 frames), canned cycles (the 810M uses `L` subroutine cycles such as L81..L89 with R parameters, not CYCLE81), arcs (I/J/K vs radius), dwell, coolant and spindle M-codes, comments, block numbers, line length and memory limits.
- Whether the EMCO VMC-200 needs anything machine-specific (tool changer, travel limits, max spindle speed).

Done means: an `assets/posts/sinumerik-810m.cps` post and a machine file for the EMCO VMC-200, with recorded golden outputs for the standard post suites (cycles, arcs, tool change, comp), a provenance line naming the public sources, and a short air-cut kit the owner can run, read back by the user.

body:
What happens (main 5fdbed9bd, after #2596's fix in PR #2638):

A 2D Chamfer with no picks, on a 60 x 40 x 10 plate that has a 1 mm modelled bevel on the X0 side only, plus a sharp 20 x 10 pocket:

- The generator classifies each top loop whole (`crates/motion/src/machining2d/chamfer_ride.rs:68-69`, one-sided vertex `gap`, line 113). The outer loop counts as bevelled, so all four outer sides are ridden, and the three sharp sides (Y0, Y40, X60) are cut at z 9.2.
- The verifier then refuses the op: `models_a_bevel` (`crates/sim/src/stock_sim/wall_anchor.rs:63-71`) fires on any bevel sample, and `crates/app/src/stock_sim_breaks.rs:144` drops all of the op's edge-break credit. Gate: `gouge: program cuts below the model in 840 cell(s), worst 0.74 mm at (1.31, 39.94, z 9.26)`.
- Without the extra collinear vertex on the bevel's top edge, the outer loop reads as sharp (gap 0, `chamfer_ride.rs:68`): the tip rides x = 1 inside the part, and the pocket rim is ridden too. Verify again refuses (1147 cells, 0.74 mm).

So the output is safe: no posted program cuts into a sharp edge. But the user gets a gouge line at a coordinate, not a reason. The op cannot be used without picking the edges, and nothing says that.

Expected:
- With no picks, ride only the modelled bevels, per segment rather than per whole loop, OR refuse at generation with a message that names the partly bevelled loop and asks for picks.
- Classify bevel vs sharp in a way that does not depend on tessellation (two-sided gap, or per segment).
- A note names the edges the op left sharp.

Found by: a blind safety review in a model trial (probes built on wopr against main; no code from the trial is proposed). Related: #2596, PR #2638.

Done means: the 60 x 40 plate with a bevel on one side posts a clean chamfer of that side only (or a named refusal that asks for picks), with and without the extra vertex; a pinning test for both; no change to the all-sharp-part behaviour (#303) or to the verifier's refusal of cuts into sharp edges.

body:
Part of #1445. Found during the fine boring work (#1479).

Fine boring (`CycleChoice::FineBore`, `CycleKind::FineBore`) posts as `G76 X Y Z R I J P F` on the Haas post only. The post engine refuses the cycle by name for each post that does not declare `fineBoring = true`. This is safe, but these controls have a fine boring cycle of their own and cannot use it.

What is owed, one control at a time:

- Fanuc, Mazak, Doosan: `G76` with `Q`. The direction of `Q` is a control parameter (Fanuc parameter No. 5101). A program cannot state it. The post can write `Q` only when the machine file states that direction, and only when the shift of the operation agrees with it. A different direction is refused by name.
- Heidenhain: `CYCL DEF 202`. It needs the spindle angle (`Q336`) and a disengaging direction code (`Q214`). The control sets the disengaging distance. The shift of the operation must map to the code, or the post refuses.
- Sinumerik: `CYCLE86`, with the lift-off path and the spindle position. The post writes the ISO dialect today.
- Mach4: `G76`. Read the word layout from the Mach4 Mill G-code manual before any word is written.
- LinuxCNC, PathPilot, grblHAL, TinyG, Carvera: no fine boring cycle. They continue to refuse.

Also owed:

- A row for `spindle.orientation` on the Machines sheet, as for `Rigid tapping`.
- `spindle.orientation` stated in the shipped machine files, where the maker's public data says it.
- A literature check of the Haas `G76` block (`I`, `J`, `P`) against the Haas Mill Operator's Manual. The session that wrote it had no web access.

Safety: a post writes the cycle only with a shift direction that the program states or that the machine file states. A post never writes a plain bore in place of a fine bore.

Done means: each control above posts the fine bore with its own word, pinned by a golden, or refuses by name with the reason; the Machines sheet shows the capability.

body:
Found during the work on #2394 (example case turning/cone-thread).

## What happens

The Profile Rough and Profile Finish rides contain runs of moves that are shorter than the output resolution of the post. The Fanuc lathe post writes them as identical consecutive `G01` blocks.

Reading: `examples/catalog/turning/cone-thread/cone-thread.nc` (PR for #2394). The program has 1197 lines. 408 of them are a `G01` block that is identical to the block before it. Example, from the finish ride where the nose comes off the collar corner onto the shoulder face:

```
G01 X28.404 Z20. F0.0333
G01 X28.402 Z20. F0.0333
G01 X28.402 Z20. F0.0333
G01 X28.402 Z20. F0.0333
G01 X28.4 Z20. F0.0333
G01 X28.4 Z20. F0.0333
(23 more identical blocks)
G01 X19.812 Z20. F0.0333
```

## Cause

`crates/motion/src/turning/offset.rs`, `profile_offset`: the chord bisection (`settle`) halves the interval toward a kink of the offset curve, where an arc meets a line or a vertical. The samples come closer than 1 micrometre. `out.dedup()` removes only samples that are exactly equal.

## Effect

- The program is correct in position.
- A control can stop for a moment at each zero-length feed block. This can leave a mark on a finished face.
- The program and the project file are larger than necessary.

## What is expected

The ride has no move shorter than a small fraction of the tolerance. Alternatively the lathe post drops a feed block whose words are equal to the last position.

Refs #2394

body:
Found during the work on #2394 (example case turning/cone-thread).

## What happens

A turned profile has a fillet that is tangent to a shoulder face. The first chords of the fillet are steep in (station, radius). The Profile Rough and Profile Finish rides go far out of the bar at the station of these chords, and come back. Each rung feeds through air.

Reading: a 30 mm bar, a collar of 30 mm diameter to Z20, a 1.2 mm fillet from the shoulder into a cone, insert `TN-1600-0R8`, stepdown 1.0, leave 0.25. The posted rough has, for each rung:

```
G00 X354.326 Z17.2
G01 X48.5 Z17.2 F0.0267
...
G01 X354.226 Z19.2 F0.05
G01 X353.936 Z19.209 F0.05
G01 X131.724 Z19.235 F0.05
G01 X87.392 Z19.278 F0.05
...
```

The rapid radius of the operation is also 177 mm, because it is the maximum radius of the outer rung. The finish ride of the same part goes out to X47.182.

The same model without the fillet (a sharp shoulder) posts a maximum of X48.6.

## Cause

`crates/motion/src/turning/offset.rs`, `profile_offset`, the closure `val`: a segment of slope `b` claims `a + b * (s - s0) + d * sqrt(1 + b * b)` at each station of its own window. That is the offset of the infinite line. For a steep, short segment the tangent point of the ball is not on the segment at these stations. The correct claim there is the circle about the nearer end point.

The first chord of the fillet has a slope of 16.6. With `d` = 10.05 the claim is 167 mm above the segment.

A vertical step is not affected: `segs` drops segments with equal stations.

## Effect

- The path is safe: the ride is too far out, never too deep.
- The program wastes time: about 300 mm of feed in air for each rung.
- On a lathe with a short X travel the limit gate refuses a legal program.
- The bisection toward the spike writes many very short moves (see the related issue about zero-length blocks).

## What is expected

The offset of a segment is limited to the stations where the tangent point is on the segment. Outside them the end point circles make the claim. The ride of a filleted shoulder stays within the nose radius plus the leave of the profile.

## Workaround

Model the shoulder as a sharp corner. The case of #2394 does this.

Refs #2394

A part has a turned profile, a thread relief neck and a modelled thread (V grooves). The Threading operation needs the V grooves in its source model. The Profile Finish operation cannot finish the same model. Its verdict reads each place that the 0.8 mm nose cannot reach as rest, and the post is blocked.

Three readings on the finished model of #2394 (cone 20 mm to 10 mm, neck 8 mm from Z60 to Z63, M10x1.5 grooves from Z63 to Z78, insert `TN-1600-0R8`):

One model is sufficient for a turned part with a neck and a thread. The profile finish cuts the major diameter and the cone up to the neck. Material that a later groove or threading operation removes (the neck, the thread valleys) does not block the profile finish.

## Workaround

Import two models on the same axis: the turned blank (no neck, no grooves) and the finished part. The facing and profile operations use the blank as source. The neck groove, the thread and the part-off use the finished part. The case of #2394 does this.

body:
Found during the work on #2394 (example case turning/cone-thread).

## What happens

A thread at the free end of a part cannot start in front of the end face. The threading verdict blocks the post.

- The thread kernel puts a V at each lattice point whose band (centre plus and minus half the insert width) overlaps the window (`crates/motion/src/turning/thread.rs`, `k_hi`).
- The meridian scan (`crates/motion/src/turning/revolve.rs`, `scan`) judges each interval that a band covers. In front of the end face the model radius is 0. The V floor is capped at the crest radius. The scan reads the difference as rest.

## Steps

1. Model a bar with a 10 mm thread diameter, 0.92 mm deep V grooves each 1.5 mm, and the end face at Z78. The last groove centre is at Z77.5.
2. Add a Threading operation with a 1.2 mm wide, 60 degree insert. Set the window top to Z78 or above.
3. Generate.

Result: `finish envelope near move 64: 0.0000 mm gouge, 5.0000 mm rest`. The post is blocked. The band of the last V (Z76.9 to Z78.1) is 0.1 mm past the end face.

A window top of Z81 gives the same result: lattice points at Z79 and Z80.5 are in free air, and the verdict reads them as 5 mm of rest.

## What is expected

A threading pass can start in free air in front of the end face. This is the usual practice: the pass starts some pitches before the part so that the spindle and the feed are synchronised. Air in front of the end face is not rest.

## Workaround

Put the last groove of the model so that the insert band ends exactly on the end face. Each pass then starts inside the part length with a feed plunge (G32 output). The case of #2394 does this: last centre at Z77.4, band Z76.8 to Z78.0.

This workaround is not safe with the G76 cycle. See the related issue "G76 cycle starts inside the part".

Refs #2394

The Threading operation starts each pass at the top lattice point of the thread. This point is always inside the length of the part. A pass cannot start in front of the end face (see the related issue about the threading verdict).

With the post option "Threading: G76 cycle", the Fanuc lathe post writes one rapid to the start point and then the two G76 blocks. The start Z is the top lattice point.

A Fanuc-type control moves the insert from the start point to the depth of each pass at rapid traverse. It does this at the start Z. At that Z the bar is solid. Thus the control moves the threading insert into the material at rapid traverse, one time for each pass.

The G32 output of the same thread does not have this problem. It writes the infeed as a `G01` block at the plunge feed.

## Example

The case turning/cone-thread of #2394, with `set_post_options { "threading": "g76" }`, posts:

```
G00 X30.1 Z77.4
G76 P010000 Q250 R0.17
G76 X8.16 Z63.9 P920 Q250 F1.5
```

The part end face is at Z78. The thread diameter is 10 mm from Z63 to Z78. At Z77.4 the insert (1.2 mm wide) stands above solid material from Z76.8 to Z78.

The golden `crates/app/tests/golden/nc/fanuc-lathe/thread_g76.nc` has the same shape: `G00 X12.1 Z14.` on a bar that continues at 12 mm diameter to Z40.

## What is expected

A G76 cycle starts in free air: in front of the end face, or in a relief groove that is wider than the insert. If the start point is above material, the post refuses the G76 cycle by name. It does not write the cycle.

## Basis

The G76 motion (rapid infeed at the start Z, feed along Z, rapid retract, rapid return) is from the public Fanuc lathe programming manuals. No machine ran this program. A person with a Fanuc lathe or simulator must confirm the reading.

## Workaround

Use G32 passes (the default). The case of #2394 does this.

Refs #2394

body:
## What

`add_operation` refuses a 2D Contour whose `params` give a lead shape that is different from the seeded shape. The message does not name the cause.

Found during the work on #2859 (example case `2d/contour-tabs`). Part of #2392.

## Steps

Run this script with `camcraft-cli script` on `upstream/main` 5fdbed9bd. A stock, a model and the tool `EM-0600-4FL` are in the document.

```js
cam.call("add_operation", {
  kind: "2D Contour",
  tool: "EM-0600-4FL",
  source: "contour-tabs",
  params: { lead: { arc: { radius: 3.0 } } }
});
```

## Result

```
camcraft-cli: call: add_operation: bad params patch: invalid value: map, expected map with a single key
```

## Cause (as read from the behaviour)

The tool applies `params` as a JSON merge patch on the seeded parameters. The seeded lead is `{ "linear": { "length": 8.0 } }`. The merged value has the two keys `linear` and `arc`. The lead is an enum with one key, so the parse fails.

## Workaround

Remove the seeded key in the same patch:

```js
params: { lead: { linear: null, arc: { radius: 3.0 } } }
```

## Expected

One of these:

- The patch replaces the lead when it names a different shape.
- The refusal names the field and the cause, for example: `lead: give one shape only (found linear and arc)`.

The same merge applies to `edit_operation` and to each parameter that is an enum with data (`links.approach.lead_out` is one). The fix must cover them.

## Done means

A test in `crates/app/tests/` gives `lead: { arc: { radius: 3.0 } }` to `add_operation` and to `edit_operation` for a 2D Contour. The operation gets the arc lead, or the refusal names `lead` and the two shapes. The `camcraft-mcp` skill says how to change a lead shape.

title: Touching solids: a face bounded only by shared edges, and the feature graph, read the shared edge as non-manifold

labels.name: bug
labels.description: Something isn't working

labels.name: area:3d
labels.description: 3D milling and finishing

labels.name: source:agent
labels.description: Opened by an AI agent (not a human reporter)

labels.name: effort:max

labels.name: P3
labels.description: Wrong behaviour a user hits, with a workaround; fix now

body:
## What happens

Since #917, the STEP reader gives each solid of a file its own facets. Two closed solids that touch along a wall can put one mesh edge into 2k facets, k in each direction.

The branch of #917 (PR B, stacked on #2843) adds one rule in `crates/geometry/src/geometry/shared_edge.rs`, `solids_touch`. The slicer (`slice_bodies::closed_solids`) and the winding check (`pick/winding.rs`) use it. The rule passes such an edge when all of these are true:

- the count is even and balanced
- each body uses the edge one time in each direction
- no apex is on the edge line
- each body has a facet on the plane of a facet of a different body

The bodies come from a link over plain edges only (two uses, one in each direction).

The rule fixes the shipped `sample_ap214.step`: it slices, and it reads as outward for Align. Two cases stay open:

1. **A face whose full boundary is shared edges.** Example: two blocks stacked face to face. The contact face of each block links to no other facet of its block over a plain edge. Thus each shared edge sees four bodies that use it one time each, and the rule refuses. Align then refuses the model as non-manifold. The slicer refuses it by name.
2. **The feature graph** (`geometry::feature::features_of_facets`) has its own edge map. It does not use the rule. On `sample_ap214.step`, 216 tangent edge pieces pick apart (`no_pickable_edge_is_a_tangent_piece_of_a_longer_one_in_any_step_fixture`).

## Rules that were tried

- **Radial pairing** (pair each facet with its angular neighbour about the edge). It failed on the sample: the solids overlap, and two facets in the same direction lie on one plane, so the order is ambiguous. It also let two cubes that meet only along one line pass, which is wrong.
- **Wall on a wall** (`solids_touch`, kept). It fails in case 1, because the bodies form before the shared edges are judged.

## Safety

Neither case gives wrong toolpath output. Each is a refusal by name, or an edge that picks in pieces. The pins:

- `shared_face_bodies::welded_non_manifold_solids_are_refused_as_a_model_fault`
- `shared_face_bodies::the_sample_laid_flat_generates_3d_finish_and_pocket_with_no_gouge`

## Wanted

- Link a face that only shared edges bound to its own solid. For example, use the STEP solid ranges (`Mesh::solid_ranges`, `app::mesh_solids`) when the model has them, or pair the coplanar opposed facets first.
- Give the feature graph the same rule.
- Remove the known-fail markers that name this issue.

body:
## What happens

The solidcore STEP path (#917, PR B on `issue/917-solidcore-step`) meshes the four-turn thread flank fixture with too many facets.

The test is `crates/app/tests/import_step_thread.rs`, `a_four_turn_thread_flank_meshes_at_full_fidelity_in_a_bounded_count`.

| Reading | Main (old reader, #1602 division) | solidcore path |
|---|---|---|
| Facets | under 5000 (the pin passes on main) | 391338 |
| Chord | 5e-3 mm | 5e-3 mm requested, replanned at 2.5e-3 mm |
| Debug test time | not measured | 93 s |

The import note is: `STEP sheet #418: replanned at 2.5e-3 mm chord to meet the requested 5e-3 mm measured tolerance`.

## Cause

At the pinned rev, solidcore-tess plans the long, thin helicoid strip isotropically. The plan at a 5 um chord measures over the tolerance. The seam then replans at half the chord (`PLAN_MARGIN`), and the count goes up again. Our seam (`crates/kernel/src/machining_mesh.rs`, `planned`) can only pick the chord. It cannot pick the shape of the division.

## Options

1. An anisotropic plan upstream in solidcore-tess: divide along the strip by the curvature of each direction.
2. A division hint through our seam: pass a per-face step in u and v to the planner, if solidcore-tess gets an API for it.

## Acceptance

The pin `facets.len() < 5_000` in the test above passes, with the other asserts of the test (chord not reduced, longest edge, area, axial gap). Until then, the test has the known-fail marker with this issue number.

Refs #917

Requested by flamingfire (Discord, relayed by the user, 2026-11-19), while setting up the helical rotor of #2772 on an A table.

## What happens

The rotary operations (Rotary Contour, Rotary Parallel, Rotary Offset) show the same Heights page as the 3-axis operations: Clearance, Retract, Top and Bottom as Z values in the setup frame (the viewport labels them, e.g. "Clearance 3.6733 (stock top +0.9843)"). On a part that turns about A, a Z plane is the wrong shape: the tool must keep its distance from the axis all the way round. The #1904 walkthrough already notes that "Bottom Z is a floor in the laid frame, not a radius".

## Wanted

For an operation on a rotary, the heights are cylinders about the fitted (or, after #2772, stated) rotary axis:

- **Clearance radius** and **retract radius**: the tool moves between cuts at this distance from the axis while A turns;
- **Top radius** / **bottom radius** (or depth from the stock skin): the radial band the passes cut, the 4-axis equivalent of Top/Bottom;
- each one offered "from stock OD", "from model max radius" or an absolute radius, the way the Z heights offer "from stock top / model top" today;
- the viewport draws them as cylinders (or circles in the axis view), not planes.

## Safety

body:
Add bounded 2D swallowtail healing via an explicit `heal_tolerance` parameter on `WireRuled` (`crates/motion/src/wire_edm/`).

## Context

Today `Region::offset_sharp` (`crates/geometry/src/geo2d.rs`) already trims local inside-corner swallowtails and bridges dead-end slots on a single 2D loop. Then `laws::cover` (`crates/motion/src/wire_edm/laws.rs`) refuses any point where `d - k > COVER_TOL` (`0.002 mm`).

## What this does

- Add `heal_tolerance: f64` (default `0.0`) to `WireRuled` (`crates/motion/src/wire_edm/ruled.rs`), distinct from twist `tolerance`.
- Refuse negative or non-finite `heal_tolerance` at the `wire_contour_ruled` door.
- Pass `reach = k + r.heal_tolerance.max(COVER_TOL)` into `laws::cover` on both planes (`ruled.rs` and `ruled_widen.rs`) while keeping `laws::kerf` (`PATH_TOL`) unchanged.
- Measure the worst uncut rest `d - k` and its location when `d - k > COVER_TOL`.
- If `d - k <= heal_tolerance`, accept the offset ring and push a clear uncut-corner note to `Toolpath::notes` naming the worst rest and spot.
- If `d - k > heal_tolerance`, keep the named refusal with the spot, measured depth `d - k`, and stated `heal_tolerance`.

## Done means:

- `wire_contour_ruled` with `heal_tolerance == 0.0` preserves all existing refusals byte for byte.
- Matching tight inside corners and shallow slots within `heal_tolerance > 0.0` generate valid paths with uncut-rest notes in `Toolpath::notes`, and paths still pass `laws::kerf`, `folds`, `crossing`, `clearance`, and `lean_law`.
- Excesses above `heal_tolerance` refuse by name with location and depth.

body:
Add a global sheet cut-order tree, hold-down sequencing, and cut-side planner in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/` (reusing the nesting rules from `crates/motion/src/plasma/nest.rs`).

Depends on #2158 and #1861.

## Scope

- Build one global containment forest across all closed contours and open chains on a nested sheet.
- Assign each open chain to its smallest enclosing closed contour, or mark it top-level when outside all parts.
- Assign each contour and chain a resolved cut role and cut side:
  - Closed loops: `Outside`, `OnLine`, or `Inside` (`Auto` sets outer part outlines to `Outside`, holes to `Inside`, and islands inside holes to `Outside`).
  - Open chains: `OnLine`, `Left`, or `Right`.
  - Refuse `Inside` or `Outside` on an open chain by name.
- Traverse the global containment tree in deterministic iterative post-order:
  - Cut internal holes, pockets, and open features of a part before its outer outline.
  - Cut small parts nested inside a hole before the enclosing hole cuts free.
  - Order sibling parts at the same depth by increasing area (small parts before large parts) to preserve router vacuum hold-down and sheet rigidity.
  - Reserve ordered pass phases: marking/scribe passes (`#1447`) first, internal/pocket passes next, rough/onion-skin profile passes next, and final onion-skin breakthrough passes last.
- Compute minimum inside-corner cutter-radius clearance diagnostics when a circular tool (`radius = cut_width / 2`) cannot reach sharp concave corners.
- Validate that no contour cuts after an enclosing contour has already freed its material.

## Done means

Tests in `crates/geometry` verify inside-out cut order across a multi-part sheet containing nested holes, internal open cuts, and a small part placed inside a large hole, verify phase ordering for marking and onion-skin passes, confirm smaller sibling parts precede larger ones deterministically, report concave inside-corner radius limits, and refuse invalid open-chain side requests by name.

body:
Add a deterministic 2D true-shape nesting kernel in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/` (no ECS, no world).

## Sources and clean room

Write this module from published literature and CamCraft code only:
- Bennell and Oliveira, *The geometry of nesting problems: a tutorial*, EJOR 2008.
- Burke, Hellier, Kendall, and Whitwell, *A new bottom-left-fill heuristic algorithm for the two-dimensional irregular packing problem*, Operations Research 2006.
- Burke, Hellier, Kendall, and Whitwell, *Complete and robust no-fit polygon generation for the irregular stock cutting problem*, EJOR 2007.
- Reuse `crates/geometry/src/geo2d.rs` (`Region`, `Loop`, `Point2`, `Region::offset_sharp`) and `crates/geometry/src/geo2d/sweep.rs` (`Region::sweep`).
- Do not read or adapt code from HSMWorks, Autodesk Fusion, WAM, SVGnest, or Deepnest.

## Scope

- Define clean input and output structs in `crates/geometry/src/nesting/`:
  - Sheet input: width, height, `edge_margin`, `cut_width` (kerf or router cutter diameter), `part_gap`, and `allow_parts_in_holes`.
  - Part input: stable part id, quantity, outer loop, hole loops, optional open chains, default cut side (`Outside`, `OnLine`, `Inside`), `rotation_mode` (`Locked`, `Orthogonal`, `FixedStep(deg)`), and `allow_mirror`.
- Inflate each part before nesting so separate cuts keep at least `part_gap` of uncut material between cut edges:
  - Inflate `Outside` outer loops by `cut_width + part_gap / 2`.
  - Inflate `OnLine` outer loops by `cut_width / 2 + part_gap / 2`.
  - Inflate `Inside` outer loops by `part_gap / 2`.
  - Buffer standalone open chains via `Region::sweep` (`cut_width / 2 + part_gap / 2` for `OnLine`, `cut_width + part_gap / 2` for side cuts).
  - Support router single-slot clearance mode (`part_gap >= cut_width`) when adjacent outside profiles share a single cutter-width channel.
- Shrink the usable sheet inward by `edge_margin` (plus outer `cut_width` clearance) via `Region::offset_sharp`.
- Compute No-Fit Polygons (NFP) and Inner-Fit Polygons (IFP) on the `geo2d::SCALE` (1-micron) grid.
- Place parts with deterministic Bottom-Left-Fill (BLF):
  - Sort parts by decreasing area first. Break ties by part id and instance index.
  - Try candidate rotations (and mirroring only when `allow_mirror` is true).
  - Place small parts inside usable closed holes (`IFP(hole_usable, part_inflated)`) when `allow_parts_in_holes` is true.
  - Open new sheets when parts do not fit on active sheets.
- Report `sheet_count`, per-sheet placed counts per part (`placed_counts`), total placed vs requested quantities, per-sheet and overall `utilization_pct` (`sum(part_net_area) / sheet_area * 100.0`), `waste_region` (`sheet_region.difference(&union_of_cut_footprints)`), used sheet bounds, and an explicit `unplaced` list with refusal reasons.
- Add the one-line provenance comment at the module head.

## Done means

Unit tests in `crates/geometry` nest irregular parts, parts with holes, and swept open chains deterministically across 1 and multiple sheets, report exact per-sheet part counts and `utilization_pct`, place a small part inside a large part hole with full clearance, confirm zero overlap among inflated footprints, verify waste `Region`, and refuse non-finite, negative, or oversized inputs by name.

body:
Part of #1445.

The first slice of #1445 (the ream, G85) left fine boring out on purpose. A fine-boring cycle stops the spindle at a fixed orientation at the bottom, shifts the tip away from the wall, then rapids out. The shift direction and amount depend on how the boring bar is clamped relative to the spindle's orientation angle. A guessed default could drag the tip across the finished bore, so no default is posted.

What is owed:
- A drill-op cycle choice for fine boring, with two required user parameters: the shift direction (or angle) and the shift amount, validated at command creation (finite, positive amount, smaller than the hole radius minus the tool's tip extent).
- A machine capability for oriented spindle stop; a machine or post without it refuses the cycle by name, never posts a plain bore in its place.
- Posts that have the canned word write it, with the shift words in that control's own form; the others refuse by name (an expanded chain needs M19-style orientation, which is per control).
- The CL chain the verifier and simulation read: feed in, (dwell), shift, rapid out, so the rapid out is judged against the wall at the shifted position.
- MCP `edit_operation` parameters for both values, a UI row in plain English.

Sources: public controller documentation only (RS-274/NGC, LinuxCNC; vendor programming manuals for the word layout). RS-274/NGC uses G76 for lathe threading; the fine-boring word differs by control and must be read from each post, not assumed.

Done means: fine boring is a user choice that posts only with an orientation-capable machine and an explicit shift, is refused by name otherwise, and is pinned by per-post goldens and a verifier test of the shifted retract.
